description: SAFe 6.0 from the architect's seat: Agile Architecture and runway, DevOps/CDP, PI Planning, solution intent and Lean Portfolio Management. For enterprise/solution/system architects preparing for the SAFe ARCH exam or working in SAFe organisations.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: How does SAFe define Agile Architecture?
notes.back: Values, practices and collaborations that support active, evolutionary design of a system — avoiding Big Design Up Front while keeping enough intentional guidance for coherence.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Agile Architecture balances which two complementary approaches?
notes.back: Emergent design (bottom-up, from teams) and intentional architecture (planned, cross-team guidance).
notes.analogy: A city: residents shape their own houses (emergent), but the council lays out roads, sewers and zoning (intentional).
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Agile Architecture; Architectural Runway

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Define emergent design — and what goes wrong with it alone at scale?
notes.back: Extending the architecture only as needed for the next increment. Alone at scale: duplicated effort, inconsistency, poor NFR performance.
notes.extra: Grounded in Agile Manifesto principle 11 (best designs emerge from self-organising teams).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Define intentional architecture.
notes.back: Purposeful, planned architectural initiatives that improve solution design and synchronise design across teams.
notes.extra: Owned mainly by System/Solution/Enterprise Architects; delivered through Enablers.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Define the Architectural Runway.
notes.back: The existing code, components and infrastructure needed to implement near-term features with minimal redesign and delay.
notes.analogy: Like an airport runway: planes (features) can only land if it is already built and long enough — and every landing wears it down.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Why must the Architectural Runway be continuously extended?
notes.back: Features consume runway as they are delivered. Without ongoing enabler investment (via capacity allocation) it shrinks and feature velocity drops.
notes.extra: Built by implementing Enablers at every level (epic → capability → feature → story).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.text:
SAFe principles of Agile Architecture:
• Design emerges. Architecture is a {{c1::collaboration}}.
• The bigger the system, the {{c2::longer the runway}}.
• Build the {{c3::simplest architecture}} that can possibly work.
• When in doubt, {{c4::code or model it out}}.
• They build it, {{c5::they test it}}.
• There is no {{c6::monopoly on innovation}}.
• Implement {{c7::architectural flow}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::01 Agile Architecture & Runway
notes.front: Rule of thumb: how far ahead should architectural enablers land relative to dependent features?
notes.back: Roughly one PI ahead, so teams find the runway in place instead of being blocked.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.text: SAFe architect roles: the {{c1::Enterprise}} Architect works at Portfolio level (technology strategy, enabler epics); the {{c2::Solution}} Architect at Large Solution level (Solution Train, Solution Intent, capabilities); the {{c3::System}} Architect at Essential level (one ART, features).
notes.extra: Main partners: EA ↔ LPM, strategic themes, Portfolio Kanban; Solution Architect ↔ Epic Owners, Solution Roadmap; System Architect ↔ Product Management, Business Owners, ART Backlog.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Enterprise Architect; Solution Architect; System Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: Who forms the leadership trio of an ART, and what does each own?
notes.back: Product Management (what), RTE (how the train runs), System Architect (how it is built).
notes.analogy: Like a ship: the owner picks the destination, the captain runs the crew, the naval architect makes sure the hull holds.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · System Architect; Agile Release Train

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: What is the leadership trio on a Solution Train?
notes.back: Solution Management, Solution Train Engineer (STE), Solution Architect.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: Core responsibilities of the Enterprise Architect in SAFe 6.0?
notes.back:
• Shape portfolio strategy and technology strategy
  • Steward enabler epics (often as Epic Owner)
  • Foster reuse and align Solution/System Architects across value streams

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: How does the architect's role change from traditional to Lean-Agile?
notes.back: From up-front gatekeeper to collaborator and coach: decentralise decisions, validate with working systems, invest in runway incrementally.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Agile Architecture; Lean-Agile Leadership

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.text: Lean-Agile Leadership has three dimensions: {{c1::Leading by example}}, {{c2::Mindset and principles}}, and {{c3::Leading change}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: How do SAFe architects collaborate across value streams?
notes.back: Through the Enterprise Architect's portfolio view, architecture Communities of Practice, shared services/platform teams, common standards and shared enabler epics.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Communities of Practice; Shared Services; Enterprise Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::02 Roles & Leadership
notes.front: Why must architects explain enablers to Business Owners in outcome terms?
notes.back: Business Owners assign business value (1–10) to PI objectives, enabler objectives included; unclear enablers get low value and lose funding.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.front: Which two bodies of knowledge make up the SAFe Lean-Agile Mindset?
notes.back: The House of Lean and the Agile Manifesto.
notes.extra: House of Lean: goal = value; pillars = respect for people and culture, flow, innovation, relentless improvement; foundation = leadership.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.text:
SAFe principles #1–#5:
#1 Take an {{c1::economic view}}
#2 Apply {{c2::systems thinking}}
#3 Assume variability; {{c3::preserve options}}
#4 Build incrementally with {{c4::fast, integrated learning cycles}}
#5 Base milestones on {{c5::objective evaluation of working systems}}

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.text:
SAFe principles #6–#10:
#6 Make value {{c1::flow without interruptions}}
#7 Apply {{c2::cadence}}, synchronize with cross-domain planning
#8 Unlock the {{c3::intrinsic motivation}} of knowledge workers
#9 {{c4::Decentralize}} decision-making
#10 Organize around {{c5::value}}

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.front: SAFe Principle #9: which decisions should an architect keep centralised?
notes.back: Infrequent, long-lasting ones with large economies of scale — e.g. technology standards, platform choice, security baselines.
notes.extra: Decentralise: frequent, time-critical decisions needing local knowledge (component design, implementation).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.front: SAFe Principle #9: which decisions should an architect decentralise to teams?
notes.back: Frequent, time-critical decisions that need local information — e.g. component design and implementation details.
notes.analogy: Head office sets the franchise standards; each restaurant decides how to handle tonight's rush.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.text: SAFe Principle #1 (economic view) trades off five variables: {{c1::lead time}}, {{c2::product cost}}, {{c3::development expense}}, {{c4::risk}} and {{c5::value}}.
notes.extra: Judge architecture on total economics, not technical elegance; sequence with Cost of Delay.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.text:
SAFe Principle #6 flow accelerators:
1. Visualize and limit {{c1::WIP}}
2. Address {{c2::bottlenecks}}
3. Minimize {{c3::handoffs and dependencies}}
4. Get {{c4::faster feedback}}
5. Work in {{c5::smaller batches}}
6. Reduce {{c6::queue lengths}}
7. Optimize time {{c7::'in the zone'}}
8. Remediate {{c8::legacy policies and practices}}
notes.extra: Architecture directly drives #3–#5: decoupling, testability, deployability.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · SAFe Principle #6 (Make value flow without interruptions)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::03 SAFe Principles & Mindset
notes.front: SAFe Principle #10: why does 'Organize around value' matter for architecture?
notes.back: Team structure and system structure mirror each other (Conway's law), so draw solution boundaries that let ARTs deliver independently.
notes.extra: The architecture must speed up, not impede, frequent independent releases across the value stream.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · SAFe Principle #10; Development Value Streams

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.text: SAFe's DevOps approach CALMR: {{c1::Culture}} of shared responsibility, {{c2::Automation}}, {{c3::Lean flow}}, {{c4::Measurement}}, {{c5::Recovery}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.text: The Continuous Delivery Pipeline has four aspects: {{c1::Continuous Exploration}} → {{c2::Continuous Integration}} → {{c3::Continuous Deployment}} → {{c4::Release on Demand}}.
notes.analogy: A restaurant: decide the menu (CE), cook and taste (CI), plate and put on the pass (CD), serve when the guest is ready (RoD).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Exploration?
notes.back: Hypothesize → Collaborate & Research → Architect → Synthesize.
notes.extra: Architect activity: design for continuous delivery, evolve runway, define enablers/NFRs, build vs buy.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Integration (SAFe CDP)?
notes.back: Develop → Build → Test end-to-end → Stage.
notes.extra: Architectural enablers: trunk-based development, test automation, decoupled components.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What are the four activities of Continuous Deployment (SAFe CDP)?
notes.back: Deploy → Verify → Monitor → Respond.
notes.extra: Architect for infrastructure as code, telemetry and fast rollback.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What are the four activities of Release on Demand?
notes.back: Release → Stabilize & Operate → Measure → Learn.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: Why should architecture decouple deployment from release?
notes.back: So code can be deployed continuously while the business decides when value is released.
notes.analogy: A film can sit finished in the cinema's projector room for weeks; the premiere date is a marketing decision.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Release on Demand; Agile Architecture

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: Name techniques that decouple deployment from release.
notes.back: Feature toggles, dark launches, canary releases, blue/green deployments, and release components on their own cadence.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Release on Demand; Agile Architecture

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What does architecting for testability involve?
notes.back: Loosely coupled components with clear interfaces, test doubles/dependency injection, observable state, and automated test hooks at every level.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Agile Architecture; Built-In Quality

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What does architecting for deployability involve?
notes.back: Infrastructure as code, small independently deployable units, backward-compatible interfaces and data migrations, and telemetry to verify deployments.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Agile Architecture; Continuous Deployment

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What is the architect's responsibility toward the System Team and pipeline?
notes.back: Define the target pipeline architecture and make the solution automatable (build, test, deploy); help execute the CDP, not just design it.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.text:
SAFe 6.0 flow metrics:
{{c1::Flow distribution}}: mix of work types (features, enablers, debt, defects)
{{c2::Flow velocity}}: items completed per period
{{c3::Flow time}}: elapsed time from start to done
{{c4::Flow load}}: items currently in progress (WIP)
{{c5::Flow efficiency}}: active time ÷ total flow time
{{c6::Flow predictability}}: planned vs actual business value
notes.extra: Architects watch distribution (share of enablers) and flow time (architectural bottlenecks).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::04 DevOps & Continuous Delivery
notes.front: What does SAFe's Built-In Quality span (dimensions)?
notes.back: Business functions, software applications, IT systems/operations, hardware, cyber-physical systems.
notes.extra: Common foundations: flow, architecture & design quality, code quality, system quality, release quality.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What is the Portfolio Vision?
notes.back: The future state of a portfolio's value streams and solutions and how they will achieve strategic themes; input to solution visions and enabler epics.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: Why should an architect read the Portfolio Canvas?
notes.back: It shows which value streams and solutions (plus value propositions, customers, budgets, KPIs) the technology strategy must serve.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Portfolio Vision (Portfolio Canvas section)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What are Strategic Themes and how does SAFe 6.0 express them?
notes.back: Differentiating business objectives that connect portfolio to enterprise strategy, expressed as OKRs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: How do strategic themes flow into architecture?
notes.back: Themes → portfolio vision → technology strategy → enabler epics → enabler capabilities/features in train backlogs → Architectural Runway.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Strategic Themes; Enterprise Architect; Enablers

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: Theme/OKR 'reduce time-to-market by 50%': how should an architect turn it into portfolio work?
notes.back: Find the architectural constraints on flow (e.g. release coupling, manual environments) → propose enabler epics with hypotheses tied to the key result → sequence them before dependent business epics.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Strategic Themes; OKRs; Enablers; Portfolio Kanban

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: Operational vs development value streams?
notes.back: Operational: deliver products/services to customers (e.g. process a loan). Development: build the solutions operational value streams use. ARTs form around development value streams.
notes.analogy: Operational = the bakery selling bread each morning; development = the team designing and maintaining the ovens.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Value Streams; Development Value Streams

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What does Value Stream Mapping measure, and how does it point to architecture work?
notes.back: Per step: process time, wait time and %C&A; overall flow time and efficiency. Long waits in integrate/test/deploy often reveal architectural constraints.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Value Stream Mapping (Continuous Delivery Pipeline)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What is an Agile Release Train (ART)?
notes.back: A long-lived team of Agile teams (~50–125 people) that plans and delivers together on a common PI cadence, around a development value stream.
notes.analogy: A train leaves on schedule: if your feature isn't on board, it waits for the next departure — the date never moves.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What is a Solution Train and when do you need one?
notes.back: Coordinates multiple ARTs and suppliers building one large, complex solution (systems of systems, often regulated).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What are Value Stream KPIs used for?
notes.back: Measuring value stream performance against business outcomes, so LPM governs value streams instead of projects.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::05 Strategy, Value Streams & Trains
notes.front: What does the architect contribute in the Value Stream and ART Identification workshop?
notes.back: Map systems to operational value streams, spot shared platforms, assess feasibility/dependencies, and propose ART boundaries that minimise cross-train coupling.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Value Stream and ART Identification (Implementation Roadmap)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What is the Solution Vision and who owns it?
notes.back: The future state of the solution (needs, capabilities, NFRs). Owned by Product/Solution Management; architects add the architecture vision.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Define Solution Intent.
notes.back: The repository of knowledge of current and intended solution behaviour (specs, designs, tests), split into fixed and variable intent.
notes.analogy: A living building dossier: as-built drawings plus the approved and still-open plans for the extension.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Fixed vs variable Solution Intent?
notes.back: Fixed: known, non-negotiable (regulations, decisions made). Variable: still open, explored via Set-Based Design. Variable becomes fixed as knowledge grows.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What is Solution Context?
notes.back: The environment the solution is deployed and used in: interfaces to other systems, hosting, regulations, usage constraints.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Solution Intent vs Solution Context: key difference?
notes.back: Intent = what the solution is and will do (inside). Context = the environment it must fit (outside) — which constrains the intent.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Solution Intent; Solution Context

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What is Set-Based Design and why does it pay off (SAFe Principle #3)?
notes.back: Keep several design options open, eliminate weaker ones as evidence arrives, commit at the last responsible moment. Avoids costly early point solutions.
notes.analogy: Like keeping two job offers alive until you know which team you really want, instead of signing the first one.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What role does MBSE play in SAFe?
notes.back: Versioned models replace documents as the main artifacts of Solution Intent, enabling simulation and early validation.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.text: SAFe work-item hierarchy: {{c1::Epic}} (portfolio) → {{c2::Capability}} (large solution) → {{c3::Feature}} (ART) → {{c4::Story}} (team).
notes.extra: Each level has a business and an enabler variant.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Epics; Capabilities; Features; Stories

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Name the four types of Enablers.
notes.back: Exploration, Architectural, Infrastructure, Compliance.
notes.extra: They exist at every backlog level.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Where do NFRs live in SAFe?
notes.back: As persistent constraints on the backlogs (not backlog items), captured in Solution Intent and verified continuously.
notes.analogy: NFRs are the building code, not a room on the floor plan: every room must meet it.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.text: A well-written NFR is {{c1::Bounded}} (context/threshold), {{c2::Independent}}, {{c3::Negotiable}} (trade-off known) and {{c4::Testable}}.
notes.extra: Anti-example: 'the system shall be fast'.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: How does SAFe handle compliance (Lean QMS)?
notes.back: Build it into the flow: capture continuous objective evidence (versioned models, automated tests, traceability) instead of end-phase documents.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What are SAFe's three roadmap horizons?
notes.back: PI roadmap (current + ~2 forecast PIs), Solution roadmap (longer, milestone-based), Portfolio roadmap (epics across value streams).
notes.extra: Architects sequence enablers so runway lands before the features that consume it.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What is capacity allocation and who negotiates it?
notes.back: A per-PI split of train capacity between features, enablers/debt and maintenance — agreed by Product/Solution Management and the System/Solution Architect.
notes.analogy: A household budget line for maintenance: without it, the roof only gets fixed after it leaks.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · ART and Solution Train Backlogs (capacity allocation)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: Distinguish the Portfolio, Solution Train and ART backlogs.
notes.back: Portfolio: approved epics (LPM). Solution Train: capabilities + enablers. ART: features + enablers for one ART. All prioritised with WSJF.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Portfolio Backlog; ART and Solution Train Backlogs

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What is the SAFe Feature format, and how do enabler features differ?
notes.back: Name + benefit hypothesis + acceptance criteria. Enabler features state a technical/flow outcome (e.g. 'deploy time 4h → 20 min').
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Features and Capabilities; Enablers

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::06 Solution Intent, Backlogs & NFRs
notes.front: What does the architect do in ART backlog refinement before PI Planning?
notes.back: Write enabler features; ensure top features have runway or a paired enabler; add NFR acceptance criteria; size for WSJF; agree capacity allocation.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · ART and Solution Train Backlogs; System Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What is PI Planning?
notes.back: A cadence-based event (usually 2 days) where all teams of an ART plan the next Planning Interval together against a shared vision.
notes.analogy: An orchestra rehearsing together before the concert instead of each musician practising alone and hoping it fits.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · PI Planning; Planning Interval

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.text: A SAFe Planning Interval typically lasts {{c1::8–12 weeks}}: commonly 4 development iterations + 1 {{c2::Innovation and Planning (IP)}} iteration.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · PI Planning; Planning Interval

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Which PI Planning Day 1 briefing belongs to the System Architect?
notes.back: Architecture vision and development practices.
notes.extra: Others: business context (Business Owner), product vision (PM), planning context (RTE).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What goes into the architecture vision briefing?
notes.back: Enablers planned for the PI, runway changes, new NFRs/constraints, development-practice expectations, and key technical dependencies.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · PI Planning; System Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What does the architect do during PI Planning team breakouts?
notes.back: Circulate: clarify enablers and NFRs, surface cross-team dependencies early, steer to the simplest design — without dictating team-level design.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Why is the architect in the Management Review and Problem-Solving session?
notes.back: To judge technical feasibility, sequence enablers, and recommend descoping features that lack runway.
notes.extra: Held end of Day 1; management adjusts scope and resolves conflicts overnight.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.text: In PI Planning, risks are ROAMed: {{c1::Resolved}}, {{c2::Owned}}, {{c3::Accepted}} or {{c4::Mitigated}}.
notes.extra: Architectural risks are often Owned by the architect or Mitigated by exploration enablers.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: How does the PI Planning confidence vote work?
notes.back: Teams, then the ART, vote fist-of-five (1–5). A low average means rework the plan; anyone voting 1–2 explains why.
notes.extra: Repeated low votes on technical items signal missing runway.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Committed vs uncommitted PI objectives?
notes.back: Committed: the team is confident it can deliver. Uncommitted: planned but uncertain — in the plan, not the commitment. Business Owners assign value (1–10) to both.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What does the ART Planning Board show, and what does the architect check on it?
notes.back: Features per team per iteration, cross-team dependencies and milestones. The architect checks enablers precede the features that consume them.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · PI Planning (ART planning board)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What is Pre-PI Planning (Solution Train)?
notes.back: Before ART PI Planning: align the solution vision, roadmap, capabilities and objectives so each ART plans within shared intent.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Pre- and Post-PI Planning

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What is Post-PI Planning (Solution Train)?
notes.back: After ART PI Planning: ARTs present plans, cross-ART risks are ROAMed, solution objectives finalised, solution confidence vote taken.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Pre- and Post-PI Planning

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: State the WSJF formula.
notes.back: WSJF = Cost of Delay ÷ Job Size (duration). Highest first.
notes.analogy: Supermarket express lane: small, urgent baskets go first because they unblock the most value per minute.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.text: In WSJF, Cost of Delay = {{c1::user-business value}} + {{c2::time criticality}} + {{c3::risk reduction / opportunity enablement (RR/OE)}}.
notes.extra: Enablers usually score high on RR/OE — that's the architect's economic case for runway.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Distinguish Iteration Review, System Demo, Solution Demo.
notes.back: Iteration Review: one team. System Demo: integrated ART increment each iteration. Solution Demo: integrated Solution Train increment, at least once per PI.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · System Demo; Solution Demo; Iteration Review

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.text: Inspect & Adapt has three parts: {{c1::PI System Demo}}, {{c2::quantitative and qualitative measurement}}, and {{c3::retrospective and problem-solving workshop}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What is the ART Sync?
notes.back: Coach Sync (Scrum Masters/Team Coaches + RTE) combined with PO Sync (POs + PM). Architects attend to surface technical dependencies and runway status.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · ART Sync (Coach Sync, PO Sync)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Which coordination events exist at the Solution Train level?
notes.back: Solution Train Sync (STE-led), plus an architect sync among System Architects led by the Solution Architect.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: What is the IP iteration used for — and what's the pitfall?
notes.back: Estimating buffer, innovation, tooling, learning, I&A and PI Planning. Pitfall: becoming the default dump for overflow work.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Innovation and Planning Iteration

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::07 PI Planning & Execution
notes.front: Key architect duties during PI execution?
notes.back:
• Guide enabler implementation and review interfaces
  • Keep NFRs tested continuously
  • Track runway consumption and technical debt

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.text: Lean Portfolio Management has three dimensions: {{c1::Strategy and Investment Funding}}, {{c2::Agile Portfolio Operations}}, {{c3::Lean Governance}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Which LPM dimension establishes Lean budgets and guardrails and maintains the portfolio vision?
notes.back: Strategy and Investment Funding.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Which LPM dimension coordinates value streams and is supported by the APMO, LACE and Portfolio Sync?
notes.back: Agile Portfolio Operations.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Which LPM dimension forecasts and budgets dynamically, measures portfolio performance and coordinates continuous compliance?
notes.back: Lean Governance.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Who are the core participants in LPM?
notes.back: Enterprise executives, Business Owners and Enterprise Architects.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Lean Portfolio Management (LPM roles)

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: How do Lean Budgets change the economics of runway vs project funding?
notes.back: Money goes to long-lived value streams, not projects, so teams own systems for life; runway and debt are funded via capacity allocation and large enabler epics.
notes.analogy: Funding a standing fire brigade instead of hiring firefighters per fire: the crew knows the town and maintains the trucks.
notes.extra: With project funding, runway is nobody's budget line and gets cut.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.text:
Lean Budget Guardrails:
1. Guide investments by {{c1::horizon}}
2. Apply {{c2::capacity allocation}}
3. Approve {{c3::significant initiatives}}
4. Continuous {{c4::Business Owner engagement}}
notes.analogy: Highway guardrails: drive as you like, just not off the cliff.
notes.extra: Guardrails 2 and 3 protect the architect's runway investment.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.text: SAFe investment horizons: Horizon 3 — {{c1::Evaluating}}; Horizon 2 — {{c2::Emerging}}; Horizon 1 — {{c3::Investing/Extracting}}; Horizon 0 — {{c4::Retiring}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Name the three main LPM events.
notes.back: Strategic Portfolio Review (strategy, budgets), Portfolio Sync (frequent progress/impediments), Participatory Budgeting (allocate budgets).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: Which LPM event for: (a) urgent cross-value-stream impediment, (b) retiring a legacy platform, (c) shifting budget to a platform enabler?
notes.back: (a) Portfolio Sync; (b) Strategic Portfolio Review; (c) Participatory Budgeting.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: What does the Enterprise Architect bring to Participatory Budgeting?
notes.back: Cost/feasibility forecasts for enabler epics and their Cost of Delay.
notes.extra: PB: stakeholders allocate the portfolio budget across value streams and epics.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::08 Lean Portfolio Management
notes.front: What is the APMO?
notes.back: The Agile Program Management Office: the evolved PMO supporting LPM, train execution and operational excellence.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: What makes something a portfolio epic?
notes.back: An initiative above the LPM cost threshold, so it needs a Lean Business Case, an MVP and LPM approval.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: What are the two types of SAFe epics?
notes.back: Business epics (customer/business value) and Enabler epics (architecture, infrastructure, exploration, compliance).

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: What does an Epic Owner do?
notes.back: Shepherds an epic through the Portfolio Kanban: hypothesis, MVP and Lean Business Case, LPM go/no-go, then supports decomposition and reports results.
notes.extra: A temporary responsibility, not a job title.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: Who is usually Epic Owner for enabler epics, and what's the hardest part?
notes.back: The Enterprise Architect. Hardest: expressing architectural value in business terms (CoD, risk reduction, flow).
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Epic Owners; Enterprise Architect

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: Structure of the Epic Hypothesis Statement?
notes.back: For [customers] who [need], the [solution] is a [how] that [value]; unlike [alternative], our solution [does better]. Plus outcomes, leading indicators, NFRs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: Key contents of a Lean Business Case?
notes.back: Hypothesis, MVP and full scope, outcomes and leading indicators, NFRs, cost forecast (MVP + full), dependencies and impacted ARTs.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: What is an MVP for a SAFe epic?
notes.back: The smallest increment that can test the epic hypothesis; leading indicators then decide persevere or pivot/stop.
notes.analogy: A pilot plant before building the full factory.
notes.extra: For enabler epics: often a thin vertical slice of the new architecture in production.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.text: Portfolio Kanban states: {{c1::Funnel}} → {{c2::Reviewing}} → {{c3::Analyzing}} → {{c4::Portfolio Backlog}} → {{c5::Implementing}} → {{c6::Done}}.
notes.analogy: Like a venture fund's pipeline: many pitches enter, few survive due diligence, funded ones must prove traction.
notes.extra: Reviewing: hypothesis + rough WSJF. Analyzing: Lean Business Case + MVP (WIP-limited). Implementing: MVP, then persevere/pivot.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::09 Epics & Portfolio Kanban
notes.front: An enabler epic exceeds the LPM threshold: who decides, and on what evidence?
notes.back: The Epic Owner (usually the EA) presents the Lean Business Case (MVP, cost, leading indicators, WSJF); Business Owners and executives in LPM decide.
notes.extra: Solution/System Architects supply feasibility and sizing, then decompose it into enabler capabilities/features.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Portfolio Kanban; Enterprise Architect; Epic Owners

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::10 Transformation
notes.text: Kotter's 8 steps (used in SAFe): 1 {{c1::sense of urgency}}; 2 {{c2::guiding coalition}}; 3 vision and strategy; 4 {{c3::communicate the vision}}; 5 empower broad-based action; 6 {{c4::short-term wins}}; 7 consolidate gains; 8 {{c5::anchor in the culture}}.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::10 Transformation
notes.text: SAFe Implementation Roadmap (abridged): reach the tipping point → train change agents → train leaders → create a {{c1::LACE}} → identify {{c2::value streams and ARTs}} → plan → prepare and {{c3::launch the ART}} → coach execution → launch more ARTs → {{c4::extend to the portfolio}} → accelerate.

notes.deck: SAFe for Architects::10 Transformation
notes.front: Why should architects join the LACE?
notes.back: So the transformation covers technical agility — DevOps, architecture for continuous delivery, enabler funding — not only process and roles.
notes.extra: LACE: small team dedicated to implementing the Lean-Agile way of working.
notes.source: SAFe ARCH · Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
